Ethan Hawke and Paul Dano duke it out as battling brothers in a disappointing revival of Sam Shepard’s fierce 1980 classic.

For this production, the Roundabout, under James Macdonald’s direction, has brought together Ethan Hawke and Paul Dano, who somehow produce all the great upheaval of a 10-gallon hat left out in a drizzle.

Hawke and Isaac are both compelling in their own ways, but they're not always compelling together, and that's a problem for a play that depends so heavily on the complex relationship between its two leads.
But while watching them go at it is entertaining, what the play is fighting for isn’t as clear.
Shepard's bracing dissection of American myths, from the idealized Western frontier to the dream of upward mobility, seemed penetrating when the play premiered in 1980.
Macdonald extracts humour from the play but the outlandish disintegration in the second act does not quite come off.
Hawke, of course, lives for this type of juicy role, playing dirty in more ways than one.
Hawke and Dano aren’t even distant cousins.
This new version, directed by James Macdonald, could use a high-voltage power infusion.
Dano is also unable to credibly execute the role reversal, which all but ruins the second half of the play, robbing it of its excitement and brutality.
But star-power short-circuits in this curiously light-hearted production from director James Macdonald at the Theatre.

Austin has grown in the years since and fancies himself a responsible family man, though what he actually does to take care of his family remains a mystery. Lee is in town because he has run out of houses to rob, and he could use a bath from the looks of him.
